Patrick Allo
Mariarosaria Taddeo

bibl.title: The ethics of algorithms: Mapping the debate

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the ethical concerns raised by decision-making algorithms, as they appear in the academic literature that discusses algorithms explicitly
span.quote: The paper answers two questions: what kinds of ethical issues are raised by algorithms? And, how do these issues apply to algorithms themselves, as opposed to technologies built upon algorithms?

span.label: what kinds of ethical issues algorithms raise, and which of them belong to the algorithm rather than to the technology built on it
span.quote: The paper answers two questions: what kinds of ethical issues are raised by algorithms? And, how do these issues apply to algorithms themselves, as opposed to technologies built upon algorithms?

span.label: a prescriptive six-part map of ethical concerns - three epistemic, two normative, one overarching - together with a review of the literature against it and an assessment of where the field is thin
span.quote: This paper makes three contributions to clarify the ethical importance of algorithmic mediation. It provides a prescriptive map to organise the debate. It reviews the current discussion of ethical aspects of algorithms. And it assesses the available literature in order to identify areas requiring further work to develop the ethics of algorithms.

span.label: method
span.quote: The map is thus not intended as a tool to help solve ethical dilemmas arising from problematic actions driven by algorithms, but rather is posed as an organising structure based on how algorithms operate that can structure future discussion of ethical issues.

span.label: the gap between how algorithms are designed and operated and how their ethical implications are understood
span.quote: This paper makes three contributions to clarify the ethical importance of algorithmic mediation. It provides a prescriptive map to organise the debate. It reviews the current discussion of ethical aspects of algorithms. And it assesses the available literature in order to identify areas requiring further work to develop the ethics of algorithms.

span.label: a conceptual map proposed a priori from how algorithms operate, then a systematic review of the literature explicitly discussing ethics of algorithms, mapped onto it
span.term: a conceptual map proposed a priori from how algorithms operate, then a systematic review of the literature explicitly discussing ethics of algorithms, mapped onto it
span.quote: We first propose a conceptual map based on six kinds of concerns that are jointly sufficient for a principled organisation of the field.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: OUTPUT CANNOT EXCEED INPUT: a conclusion inherits the reliability and the non-neutrality of the data it was computed from, so an algorithm cannot repair evidence that was misguided before it arrived
span.note: status: the informal ‘garbage in, garbage out’ principle clearly illustrates
span.quote: the informal ‘garbage in, garbage out’ principle clearly illustrates what is at stake here, namely that conclusions can only be as reliable (but also as neutral) as the data they are based on.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A LEARNING ALGORITHM REWRITES ITS OWN DECISION STRUCTURE WHILE RUNNING, so the rationale for any particular classification is not fixed at design time and cannot be read off the program
span.quote: The algorithm modifies its behavioural structure during operation ( Markowetz et al., 2014). This alteration of how the algorithm classifies new inputs is how it learns

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ONCE TRAINED, CLASSIFICATION PROCEEDS WITHOUT AN OPERATOR - the structure produced by training is what new inputs meet, which is why oversight has no natural point of entry
span.quote: Training produces a structure (e.g. classes, clusters, ranks, weights, etc.) to classify new inputs or predict unknown variables. Once trained, new data can be processed and categorised automatically without operator intervention

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: POPULATION KNOWLEDGE APPLIED TO AN INDIVIDUAL: correlations hold of groups while the action lands on a person, and even population-level action spills over - an insurance premium set for a sub-population is paid by each member
span.quote: even if both actions and knowledge are at the population-level, our actions may spill over into the individual level. For example, this happens when an insurance premium is set for a sub-population, and hence has to be paid by each member.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: VALUES ENTER THROUGH PARAMETERS: developers specify and users configure operational parameters with desired outcomes in mind, so the algorithm privileges some interests before it processes anything
span.quote: Operational parameters are specified by developers and configured by users with desired outcomes in mind that privilege some values and interests over others

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SECRECY IS COMMERCIALLY MOTIVATED, NOT INCIDENTAL: disclosure would enable gaming and threaten viability, so inaccessibility is a position taken in a conflict of interests rather than a technical limit
span.quote: This struggle is marked by information asymmetry and an “imbalance in knowledge and decision-making power” favouring data processors

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: CORRELATIONS ARE ACTED ON WITHOUT CAUSAL KNOWLEDGE because a sufficient volume of data is treated as credible enough to drive action - the paper's name for that lowered bar is `actionable insights`
span.quote: In this sense data mining and profiling algorithms often need only establish a sufficiently reliable evidence base to drive action, referred to here as actionable insights.

span.label: the review covers only literature that discusses algorithms explicitly, so neighbouring fields - AI ethics, surveillance studies, computer ethics, machine ethics - are touched on only briefly
span.quote: The review undertaken here was primarily limited to literature explicitly discussing algorithms. As a result, much relevant work performed in related fields is only briefly touched upon, in areas such as ethics of artificial intelligence, surveillance studies, computer ethics and machine ethics.

span.label: the authors accept there may be gaps in coverage for topics discussed only in relation to specific algorithm types rather than to algorithms as such
span.quote: We must therefore accept that there may be gaps in coverage for topics discussed only in relation to specific types of algorithms, and not for algorithms themselves.

span.label: summarising every field in which algorithms are used is stated to be beyond reach, and the narrowing is justified on that ground
span.quote: While it would be ideal to summarise work in all the fields represented in the reviewed literature, and thus in any domain where algorithms are in use, the scope of such as an exercise is prohibitive.

span.label: discussion of 'algorithm' runs into a level-of-abstraction problem: without fixing the level, parties talk past each other and the set of relevant observables is never bounded
span.quote: Discussion of a concept as complex as ‘algorithm’ inevitably encounters problems of abstraction or ‘talking past each other’ due to a failure to specify a level of abstraction (LoA) for discussion, and thus limit the relevant set of observables

span.label: the authors state that a mature ethics of algorithms does not yet exist, and attribute that partly to the breadth of the concept itself
span.quote: A mature ‘ethics of algorithms’ does not yet exist, in part because ‘algorithm’ as a concept describes a prohibitively broad range of software and information systems.

span.label: configuration is excluded from changing the object: tuning an algorithm to a task is said not to alter its mathematical representation or its implementation, which bounds what the map is about
span.quote: the configuration of an algorithm to a specific task or dataset does not change its underlying mathematical representation or system implementation; it is rather a further tweaking of the algorithm's operation in relation to a specific case or problem.

span.label: algorithms that automate mundane tasks are excluded by declaration rather than by a criterion, and the class of interest is given without a precise definition
span.quote: Algorithms that automate mundane tasks, for instance in manufacturing, are not our concern.

span.label: the paper marks its own normative judgements as observer-dependent rather than claiming a standard: whether evidence counts as misguided, and whether an outcome counts as unfair, are both said to depend on who is evaluating
span.note: eliminates: a reader taking the map's normative labels as the authors' own ethical standard - `misguided` and `unfair` are marked observer-dependent, so the framework cannot be read as smuggling in a particular ethics · outcome: held
span.quote: Evaluations of the neutrality of the process, and by connection whether the evidence produced is misguided, are of course observer-dependent.

span.label: the map is declared not to derive from any particular ethical theory, which is what lets readers who disagree about ethics still use it
span.note: eliminates: the objection that the map only works for readers who already share the authors' ethical theory - it is declared to derive from none · outcome: held
span.quote: The map is not proposed from a particular theoretical or methodological approach to ethics, but rather is intended as a prescriptive framework of types of issues arising from algorithms owing to three aspects of how algorithms operate.

span.label: algorithm
span.quote: we follow Hill's ( 2015: 47) formal definition of an algorithm as a _mathematical construct_ with “a finite, abstract, effective, compound control structure, imperatively given, accomplishing a given purpose under given provisions.”

span.label: actionable insights
span.quote: In this sense data mining and profiling algorithms often need only establish a sufficiently reliable evidence base to drive action, referred to here as actionable insights.

span.label: transparency
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: accessibility
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: comprehensibility
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: traceability
span.quote: Such difficulties motivate the addition of _traceability_ as a final, overarching, concern.

span.label: data analytics
span.quote: The discipline of data analytics is a standout example, defined here as the practice of using algorithms to make sense of streams of data.

span.label: practice
span.quote: The discipline of data analytics is a standout example, defined here as the practice of using algorithms to make sense of streams of data.

span.label: profiling
span.quote: Algorithmic activities, like profiling, reontologise the world by understanding and conceptualising it in new, unexpected ways, and triggering and motivating actions based on the insights it generates.

span.label: information asymmetry
span.quote: This struggle is marked by information asymmetry and an “imbalance in knowledge and decision-making power” favouring data processors

span.label: level of abstraction
span.quote: Discussion of a concept as complex as ‘algorithm’ inevitably encounters problems of abstraction or ‘talking past each other’ due to a failure to specify a level of abstraction (LoA) for discussion, and thus limit the relevant set of observables

span.label: correlations
span.quote: statistical methods can help identify significant correlations, but these are rarely considered to be sufficient to posit the existence of a causal connection ( Illari and Russo, 2014: Chapter 8), and thus may be insufficient to motivate action on the basis of knowledge of such a connection.

span.label: causal connection
span.quote: statistical methods can help identify significant correlations, but these are rarely considered to be sufficient to posit the existence of a causal connection ( Illari and Russo, 2014: Chapter 8), and thus may be insufficient to motivate action on the basis of knowledge of such a connection.

span.label: machine learning
span.quote: The rationale of the algorithm is obscured, lending to the portrayal of machine learning algorithms as ‘black boxes’.

span.label: opacity
span.quote: the different concerns are part of a web of interdependencies. Some of these interdependencies are present in the literature we reviewed, like the connection between bias and discrimination (see ‘Misguided evidence leading to bias’ and ‘Unfair outcomes leading to discrimination’ sections) or the impact of opacity on the attribution of responsibility (see ‘Inscrutable evidence leading to opacity’ and ‘Traceability leading to moral responsibility’ sections).

span.label: bias
span.quote: the different concerns are part of a web of interdependencies. Some of these interdependencies are present in the literature we reviewed, like the connection between bias and discrimination (see ‘Misguided evidence leading to bias’ and ‘Unfair outcomes leading to discrimination’ sections) or the impact of opacity on the attribution of responsibility (see ‘Inscrutable evidence leading to opacity’ and ‘Traceability leading to moral responsibility’ sections).

span.label: discrimination
span.quote: Better methods to produce evidence for some actions need not rule out all forms of discrimination for example, and can even be used to discriminate more efficiently.

span.label: responsibility
span.quote: the different concerns are part of a web of interdependencies. Some of these interdependencies are present in the literature we reviewed, like the connection between bias and discrimination (see ‘Misguided evidence leading to bias’ and ‘Unfair outcomes leading to discrimination’ sections) or the impact of opacity on the attribution of responsibility (see ‘Inscrutable evidence leading to opacity’ and ‘Traceability leading to moral responsibility’ sections).

span.label: implementation
span.quote: Lay usage of ‘algorithm’ also includes _implementation_ of the mathematical construct into a technology, and an application of the technology _configured_ for a particular task.

span.label: privacy
span.quote: Transparency can thus run counter to other ethical ideals, in particular the privacy of data subjects and autonomy of organisations.

span.label: algorithm - THE PAPER HOLDS TWO SENSES AT ONCE AND SAYS SO. The formal sense is Hill's mathematical construct; the sense it actually maps is the public-discourse one, which includes the implementation into a technology and the configuration of that technology to a task. Its own point is that a map of the ethics cannot use the formal sense alone
span.quote: Lay usage of ‘algorithm’ also includes _implementation_ of the mathematical construct into a technology, and an application of the technology _configured_ for a particular task.

span.label: algorithm - AND THE CONFLATION IS NAMED AS THE OBSTACLE, not glossed over: the same word carries a mathematical construct and 'any procedure or decision process, however ill-defined', and the paper says the mapping exercise must address that before it can begin
span.quote: Any attempt to map an ‘ethics of algorithms’ must address this conflation between formal definitions and popular usage of ‘algorithm’.

span.label: transparency - NOT ONE PROPERTY BUT TWO CONDITIONS THAT COME APART: information can be accessible and still not comprehensible, which is exactly the case machine learning creates
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: fairness - EXPLICITLY OBSERVER-DEPENDENT HERE, a generic label for whatever ethical criteria an observer brings to the action rather than a standard the paper supplies
span.quote: ethical evaluation of algorithms can also focus solely on the _action_ itself. Actions driven by algorithms can be assessed according to numerous ethical criteria and principles, which we generically refer to here as the observer-dependent ‘fairness’ of the action and its effects.

span.label: inconclusive evidence - THE PAPER'S OWN CATEGORY, defined as the uncertainty that is inherent rather than accidental: inferential and machine-learning methods yield knowledge that is probable and inevitably uncertain, so the deficiency cannot be engineered away
span.quote: When algorithms draw conclusions from the data they process using inferential statistics and/or machine learning techniques, they produce probable6 yet inevitably uncertain knowledge.

span.label: inscrutable evidence - defined by a REASONABLE EXPECTATION THAT IS NOT MET: the link between data and conclusion ought to be intelligible and open to scrutiny, and given how algorithms operate that is not automatically satisfied
span.quote: When data are used as (or processed to produce) evidence for a conclusion, it is reasonable to expect that the connection between the data and the conclusion should be accessible (i.e. intelligible as well as open to scrutiny and perhaps even critique).

span.label: misguided evidence - defined from a limit shared by ALL data processing rather than anything specific to algorithms: the output can never exceed the input
span.quote: Algorithms process data and are therefore subject to a limitation shared by all types of data-processing, namely that the output can never exceed the input.

span.label: transformative effects - the category for harms with NO IDENTIFIABLE VICTIM AND NO OBVIOUS FAILURE: effects that look ethically neutral because nothing was broken, yet change how the world is conceptualised and organised
span.quote: algorithms can affect how we conceptualise the world, and modify its social and political organisation

span.label: critiques → the treatment of distinct epistemic and normative concerns as a single cluster, so that fixing one is taken to address the rest
span.quote: the map demonstrates that solving problems at one level does not address all types of concerns; a perfectly auditable algorithmic decision, or one that is based on conclusive, scrutable and well-founded evidence, can nevertheless cause unfair and transformative effects, without obvious ways to trace blame among the network of contributing actors.

span.label: critiques → the assumption that better evidence reduces discrimination - the paper holds that it can be used to discriminate more efficiently
span.quote: Better methods to produce evidence for some actions need not rule out all forms of discrimination for example, and can even be used to discriminate more efficiently.

span.label: predicts → the expectation that increasingly better algorithmic tools will eliminate the ethical problems of algorithms
span.quote: we cannot in principle avoid epistemic and ethical residues.

span.label: critiques → the naive treatment of transparency as a panacea for ethical issues arising from new technologies
span.quote: transparency is often naïvely treated as a panacea for ethical issues arising from new technologies.

span.label: qualifies → the assumption that a more discerning algorithm is the ethically preferable one
span.quote: one may even conceive of situations where less discerning algorithms may have fewer objectionable effects.

span.label: correlations —distinct-from→ causal connection
span.quote: statistical methods can help identify significant correlations, but these are rarely considered to be sufficient to posit the existence of a causal connection ( Illari and Russo, 2014: Chapter 8), and thus may be insufficient to motivate action on the basis of knowledge of such a connection.

span.label: accessibility —part-of→ transparency
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: comprehensibility —part-of→ transparency
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: transparency —contrasted-with→ privacy
span.quote: Transparency can thus run counter to other ethical ideals, in particular the privacy of data subjects and autonomy of organisations.

span.label: machine learning —causes→ opacity
span.quote: The longstanding problem of interpretability in machine learning algorithms indicates the challenge of opacity in algorithms

span.label: implementation —part-of→ algorithm
span.quote: Lay usage of ‘algorithm’ also includes _implementation_ of the mathematical construct into a technology, and an application of the technology _configured_ for a particular task.

span.label: data analytics —is-a→ practice
span.quote: The discipline of data analytics is a standout example, defined here as the practice of using algorithms to make sense of streams of data.

span.label: six kinds of concern are proposed as jointly sufficient to organise the field: three epistemic, two normative and traceability as an overarching one
span.quote: This leads us to posit three epistemic, and two normative kinds of ethical concerns arising from the use of algorithms, based on how algorithms process data to produce evidence and motivate actions.

span.label: solving a problem at one level of the map leaves the other kinds untouched
span.quote: the map demonstrates that solving problems at one level does not address all types of concerns; a perfectly auditable algorithmic decision, or one that is based on conclusive, scrutable and well-founded evidence, can nevertheless cause unfair and transformative effects, without obvious ways to trace blame among the network of contributing actors.

span.label: the concerns are interdependent, and two links were already present in the literature: bias with discrimination, and opacity with the attribution of responsibility
span.quote: the different concerns are part of a web of interdependencies. Some of these interdependencies are present in the literature we reviewed, like the connection between bias and discrimination (see ‘Misguided evidence leading to bias’ and ‘Unfair outcomes leading to discrimination’ sections) or the impact of opacity on the attribution of responsibility (see ‘Inscrutable evidence leading to opacity’ and ‘Traceability leading to moral responsibility’ sections).

span.label: acting on correlations is doubly problematic - the correlation may be spurious, and even a genuine one holds of populations while the action is directed at individuals
span.quote: Even if strong correlations or causal knowledge are found, this knowledge may only concern populations while actions are directed towards individuals

span.label: algorithm
span.quote: we follow Hill's ( 2015: 47) formal definition of an algorithm as a _mathematical construct_ with “a finite, abstract, effective, compound control structure, imperatively given, accomplishing a given purpose under given provisions.”

span.label: transparency
span.quote: Transparency is generally defined with respect to “the availability of information, the conditions of accessibility and how the information … may pragmatically or epistemically support the user's decision-making process”

span.label: data analytics
span.quote: The discipline of data analytics is a standout example, defined here as the practice of using algorithms to make sense of streams of data.

span.label: actionable insights
span.quote: In this sense data mining and profiling algorithms often need only establish a sufficiently reliable evidence base to drive action, referred to here as actionable insights.

span.label: traceability
span.quote: harm caused by algorithmic activity is hard to debug (i.e. to detect the harm and find its cause), but also that it is rarely straightforward to identify who should be held responsible for the harm caused.

span.label: accessibility of information about an algorithm
span.term: accessibility of information about an algorithm
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.

span.label: comprehensibility of that information
span.quote: The primary components of transparency are _accessibility_ and _comprehensibility_ of information.
